text: - egy may be appropriate in those at lower risk. • Additional antiplatelet therapy with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors may have a role in patients treated invasively or conservatively.47 Benefit has been established in pa- tients undergoing PCI (see Reperfusion and Revascular- isation Procedures, p.1181), but results in patients treat- ed medically have been less consistent. A meta- analysis48 of studies of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in unstable angina or non-ST elevation myocardial infarc- tion found that they reduced the risk of death or myocar- dial infarction in patients who were not scheduled for early revascularisation, particularly in those at high risk of progression, such as those with raised troponins. However, many of the patients included in the analysis did receive revascularisation and the use of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in patients not undergoing interven- tion remains questionable.21 Whether all the glycopro- tein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are effective is also unclear. For patients not undergoing PCI, individual studies have re- ported beneficial results with tirofiban and aspirin, alone49 or in combination with heparin therapy,50 and with eptifibatide51 in addition to standard therapy, but not with abciximab52 in addition to aspirin and heparin. The benefit of treatment with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa in- hibitors in patients already taking aspirin and clopidog- rel is also not yet established.53,54 • The use of statins early after admission for acute coro- nary syndromes has been recommended,23 although meta-analyses have come to differing conclusions re- garding their benefit. One analysis55 found early use of statins had no effect on outcomes at 1 or 4 months after the initial event, but another56 reported a reduction in cardiovascular events with statin therapy for 6 months or longer; benefit may be increased with high-dose reg- imens.57 After discharge, patients should continue to take aspirin and a beta blocker; clopidogrel should also continue to be added to aspirin for up to 9 to 12 months.21,23,58 Statins should also be continued, and other measures to reduce cardiovascular risk should be adopted. Anti-ischaemic drugs should be given as required; some patients are given a long-acting nitrate for long-term prophylaxis, although nitrates have not been shown to protect against subsequent cardiovascular events. Long-term oral anticoagulation has been used but is not routine therapy, and studies of warfa- rin with aspirin have given mixed results.59,60 Prolonged use of low-molecular-weight heparins has been investigat- ed,61,62 but benefit has not been confirmed. Treatment of Prinzmetal’s angina. This should be treat- ed like unstable angina with the addition of a calcium- channel blocker; the selection of an appropriate calcium- channel blocker is described above under the treatment of stable angina.
